summary: Describes an optional, backward-compatible cryptographic authentication mechanism for Babel routing using HMAC and two new TLV types. It updates RFC 6126 and was replaced by RFC 8967.

plainLanguage.summary: A routing message can carry a secret stamp proving who sent it. This was an early way to do it and has since been replaced.

questions: how does babel authenticate routing messages
what is a security association in routing
how to prevent replay attacks in routing
subtitle: Adding optional cryptographic authentication to Babel routing protocol messages.

tldr.problem: Babel routing protocol messages can be forged or modified by attackers, and there is no way to verify that routing information comes from trusted sources.
tldr.mechanism: This extension adds optional HMAC-based authentication to Babel packets using secret keys shared between routers. Each packet includes a cryptographic sequence number for replay protection and HMAC values computed over the packet content.
tldr.outcome: Authentication became available for Babel networks but this experimental mechanism was replaced by RFC 8967, which defines a more robust authentication method.

today: RFC 7298 added experimental authentication to the Babel routing protocol. It has been replaced by RFC 8967, which provides a more robust authentication mechanism for Babel.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Babel is a distance-vector routing protocol designed for wireless mesh networks. Like all routing protocols, it exchanges messages about network paths and reachability. Without authentication, attackers could inject false routing information, redirect traffic, or cause network disruption.

This RFC defines an optional authentication extension for Babel that is backward compatible: routers without authentication enabled can coexist with authenticated routers on the same network. The mechanism follows established practices from other routing protocol authentication systems (RIP, OSPF, ISIS) by using HMAC (Hashed Message Authentication Code) with a cryptographic sequence number to prevent replay attacks.

A key design goal is to make the authentication parameters and their security implications clear and predictable to network operators, even when implementation details vary.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing protocols tell routers how to reach other networks. This extension lets routers prove to each other that they know a shared secret, so attackers cannot trick them with fake routing information.

sections.title: Cryptographic Mechanism
sections.content:
The extension uses HMAC, a construction that combines a cryptographic hash function with a secret key. The RFC mandates support for two hash algorithms: RIPEMD-160 and SHA-1 (both producing 160-bit digests), and allows optional support for stronger algorithms like SHA-256 and SHA-512.

Each authenticated packet includes two critical elements: a cryptographic sequence number to detect replayed old messages, and an HMAC value computed over the meaningful parts of the packet using a shared secret key. The sequence number is monotonically increasing and wraps around after reaching its maximum value, which operators can observe to understand the strength of replay protection.

Before computing the HMAC, the packet is padded: HMAC placeholder fields are initialized with a padding constant (typically zero), and the first 16 octets of the HMAC TLV are replaced with the source address to protect against source address spoofing. After HMAC computation, the real HMAC value is inserted into the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism mixes a secret password with the routing message through a special mathematical formula, creating a unique stamp that proves you know the password. A counter makes sure you are not replaying an old message.

sections.title: Protocol Extensions
sections.content:
The RFC updates Babel's protocol data structures and encoding to support authentication. Each interface has local state including the current timestamp (local sequence number) and packet counter (PC) for outgoing packets. The RxAuthRequired flag indicates whether the interface requires incoming packets to be authenticated.

Two new TLV (Type-Length-Value) parameter types are defined: TS/PC TLV contains the timestamp and packet counter, appearing exactly once in each authenticated packet. The HMAC TLV contains the HMAC computation result, and multiple HMAC TLVs can appear in a single packet to support authentication with multiple keys or hash algorithms (for example, allowing gradual migration between keys).

The protocol supports Configured Security Associations (CSAs), which specify authentication keys and parameters, and derives Effective Security Associations (ESAs) from them based on the current time and interface state. This allows operators to schedule key transitions in advance without disrupting the network.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension adds two types of stamps to routing messages: one that says when the message was sent and a counter, and one or more stamps that prove you know the secret key.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving
sections.content:
When sending an authenticated packet, the router inserts a TS/PC TLV with the current sequence number and packet counter. It then computes the HMAC over the entire HIP header and data (excluding the HMAC TLVs themselves) using each configured authentication key, and appends the HMAC TLVs to the packet.

The RFC defines strict limits on how many HMAC computations are performed: per outgoing packet, the router computes at most MaxDigestsOut HMACs (typically a small number like 2 or 3), limiting computational overhead. When there are more configured keys than the limit, the most recently active keys are preferred.

When receiving an authenticated packet, the router verifies the TS/PC TLV and checks that the sequence number is fresh (not a replay). It then attempts to validate each HMAC TLV using known authentication keys. At most MaxDigestsIn HMAC validations are tried per packet, limiting the CPU cost of reception. If no valid HMAC is found and authentication is required on that interface, the packet is dropped. Routers maintain per-interface statistics tracking authentication events, allowing operators to diagnose configuration problems.
sections.plainLanguage: When sending, the router adds a timestamp and stamp. When receiving, the router checks the timestamp is new (not old) and verifies the stamp matches one of the passwords it knows.

sections.title: Deployment and Management
sections.content:
The extension is fully backward compatible. Unauthenticated routers and authenticated routers can coexist on the same network. A network can gradually transition to authentication by configuring CSAs on some interfaces ahead of time, then activating them at a coordinated moment. During transition, both authenticated and unauthenticated packets can be accepted on the same interface.

A router can simultaneously authenticate within multiple security domains by using different keys and hash algorithms in separate HMAC TLVs, allowing large networks to migrate specific regions without global coordination.

To prevent key exhaustion, the sequence number space is large (32 bits, allowing over 4 billion packets), and the RFC defines handling for when the sequence number wraps around: a new key must be configured to continue authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks can add authentication gradually. Old routers keep working while new ones authenticate. Multiple groups of routers can use different passwords at the same time on the same network.
